description.summary: An extensive group of pre-Columbian geoglyphs scratched into the desert pampa between the towns of Nazca and Palpa in southern Peru, created by the Paracas and Nazca cultures roughly between 500 BCE and 500 CE. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.
description.full: The Nazca Lines are an extensive group of geoglyphs scored into the surface of the Pampas de Jumana plateau in southern Peru, between the towns of Nazca and Palpa about 400 km south of Lima. The site covers roughly 50 km² and contains lines whose combined length exceeds 1,300 km. The geoglyphs were created in two principal phases — a Paracas-culture phase (c. 400–200 BCE) and a Nazca-culture phase (c. 200 BCE – 500 CE) — by removing the reddish-brown ferric-oxide-coated pebbles of the desert pavement to expose the lighter subsoil beneath. Most lines are 10–15 cm deep and around 33 cm wide, with some up to 1.8 m wide. The figures include geometric shapes, plant motifs, and hundreds of zoomorphic and anthropomorphic designs, the most famous including a 93 m hummingbird, a 134 m condor, a 93×58 m monkey, and a 47 m spider. The Lines were first noted in modern times by the Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejía Xesspe in 1927 and were systematically studied from 1940–41 by the American historian Paul Kosok and from the 1940s onward by the German mathematician Maria Reiche. They were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. Major scholarly debates concern whether the lines functioned as an astronomical calendar (Kosok, Reiche), as ritual pathways or shamanistic features, or as indicators tied to underground water sources (Reinhard, Johnson). Recent decades have seen the discovery of hundreds of additional geoglyphs through aerial survey, drones, satellite imagery, and machine-learning analysis, including a 2019 announcement of 143 new geoglyphs identified in collaboration between Yamagata University and IBM Japan, and the 2020 discovery of a giant cat figure on a steep hillside.

features.description: Long straight lines and trapezoidal cleared areas, some over 1,300 km in combined length
Hundreds of animal figures, including hummingbird (93 m), condor (134 m), monkey (93×58 m), spider (47 m), and others (whale, dog, lizard, parrot, pelican, heron, killer whale, cat)
Human or human-like figures (e.g. the 'astronaut' or 'owl-man' on a hillside)
Plant designs and geometric trapezoids and spirals
Created by removing reddish iron-oxide-coated surface pebbles to expose lighter subsoil; lines typically 10–15 cm deep and ~33 cm wide, with some up to 1.8 m wide

physical.morphology: An ensemble of geoglyphs across a 50 km² desert pampa, executed at scales ranging from small motifs to figures hundreds of metres across, only fully legible from the air or from surrounding hilltops.

range.description: Concentrated in the arid Pampas de Jumana plateau between Nazca and Palpa in southern Peru, approximately 400 km south of Lima.

hotspots.name: Pampas de Jumana / Nazca-Palpa plateau

location.description: Pampas de Jumana plateau between the towns of Nazca and Palpa, Ica Region

hotspots.notes: Core area of the Nazca Lines, covering approximately 50 km² with combined line length exceeding 1,300 km

first_recorded.source: First modern record by Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejía Xesspe

peak_activity_periods.description: Earlier phase of geoglyph construction by the Paracas culture
Main phase of geoglyph construction by the Nazca culture

origins.cultural_roots: Created by the Paracas culture and especially the Nazca culture of the south-coastal Andes, on a desert pavement that preserves shallow lines for millennia.
origins.earliest_accounts: Created c. 400 BCE – 500 CE; first modern scholarly notice by Toribio Mejía Xesspe in 1927.
origins.folklore_connections: Embedded in the wider tradition of pre-Columbian Andean ritual landscapes.

timeline.event: Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejía Xesspe first records the Nazca Lines in modern scholarship
timeline.significance: Beginning of formal study of the geoglyphs

timeline.event: American historian Paul Kosok begins systematic field study of the Nazca Lines
timeline.significance: Initiation of the astronomical / calendrical hypothesis

timeline.event: Erich von Däniken publishes Chariots of the Gods?, popularizing the extraterrestrial-runway hypothesis for the Nazca Lines
Gerald Hawkins and Anthony Aveni conclude that 'the evidence was insufficient to support' the astronomical-calendar hypothesis
timeline.significance: Mainstream archaeoastronomical critique of the Reiche hypothesis

timeline.event: UNESCO inscribes the Lines and Geoglyphs of Nazca and Pampas de Jumana on the World Heritage List (18th Session, criteria i, iii, iv)
timeline.significance: Formal international recognition of the site's outstanding universal value

timeline.event: Greenpeace activists damage the area around the hummingbird geoglyph during a protest banner stunt
timeline.significance: Major modern conservation incident; one activist was later convicted

timeline.event: Yamagata University and IBM Japan announce 143 new geoglyphs identified using machine-learning analysis
timeline.significance: First major application of AI to Nazca survey

timeline.event: Discovery of a giant cat figure on a steep hillside in the Nazca complex
timeline.significance: Notable individual discovery, dated stylistically to the late Paracas period

timeline.event: AI-assisted survey announces 303 previously unknown geoglyphs depicting parrots, cats, monkeys, killer whales, and severed heads
timeline.significance: Largest single expansion of the known corpus

history.modern_era: The Nazca Lines remain a focus of active archaeological research, conservation effort, and public interest. The total number of recognized geoglyphs has expanded markedly through the 21st century via aerial photography, drones, satellite imagery, and machine-learning surveys; the site faces ongoing pressures from climate change, illegal mining, infrastructure incidents, and tourism.

physical.name: Nazca Lines geoglyph corpus
physical.description: More than 350 documented geoglyphs (with hundreds more added through 21st-century AI-assisted surveys), including linear, geometric, zoomorphic, and anthropomorphic figures spread across the Pampas de Jumana.
physical.location: Pampas de Jumana, Nazca and Palpa Provinces, Ica Region, Peru
physical.analysis: Extensively documented by Mejía Xesspe (1927), Kosok (1940s), Reiche, Reinhard, the Yamagata University team (since 2006), and IBM Japan (2019 onward). UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994.
physical.source: Multiple peer-reviewed and institutional studies; UNESCO inscription

photographic.name: Aerial photographic record of the Nazca Lines
photographic.description: Comprehensive aerial documentation of the geoglyphs from the 1940s onwards, including Maria Reiche's mapping efforts.
photographic.analysis: Aerial photography has been the primary documentary medium for the site since the geoglyphs are most legible from the air.

paranormal.name: Extraterrestrial-runway hypothesis (von Däniken, 1969)
paranormal.description: Erich von Däniken's 1969 Chariots of the Gods? proposed that the Nazca Lines were runways or markers built for or by ancient extraterrestrial visitors.
evidence_cited: Visibility of figures from above only

scientific.name: Astronomical / calendrical hypothesis (Kosok and Reiche)
scientific.description: Hypothesis that the Lines functioned as an astronomical observatory or calendar, marking solstices, equinoxes, and other celestial alignments.
evidence_cited: Apparent solstice alignments of selected lines

scientific.name: Water and fertility hypothesis (Reinhard, Johnson)
scientific.description: Johan Reinhard proposed the lines were tied to water worship and fertility ritual, with figures symbolizing deities of agricultural success. David Johnson argued some geoglyphs align with subterranean aquifers and aqueduct (puquio) systems.
evidence_cited: Alignment of certain geoglyphs with puquio aqueducts

scientific.name: Ritual pathway / pilgrimage hypothesis
scientific.description: Many lines functioned as ceremonial pathways walked during ritual pilgrimages, with different geoglyph groups serving distinct functions (calendrical, fertility, processional).
evidence_cited: Wear patterns consistent with foot traffic
Ethnographic parallels with later Andean ritual practice

skeptical.name: Insufficient evidence for astronomical hypothesis
skeptical.description: Gerald Hawkins (1968) and Anthony Aveni (1990) concluded the evidence was insufficient to support the astronomical-calendar interpretation as a primary function for the lines.
evidence_cited: Statistical analysis of line orientations did not exceed chance expectations for simple solar alignments

skeptical.name: Nickell reproduction (debunking the extraterrestrial hypothesis)
skeptical.description: Investigator Joe Nickell demonstrated that period-appropriate tools and methods are sufficient to reproduce Nazca-style figures at scale, undercutting any need for extraterrestrial explanation.

folklore.beliefs: The geoglyphs are now embedded in modern Peruvian national heritage and global popular culture; their original ritual meanings are reconstructed only through archaeology.

indigenous.significance: The geoglyphs are products of long-standing Indigenous Andean ritual landscapes. Modern descendant communities and the Peruvian state regard the site as a major cultural heritage.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Pseudoscientific framings (e.g. extraterrestrial-runway hypotheses) erase the achievements of the Paracas and Nazca peoples; mainstream scholarship attributes the geoglyphs entirely to these Indigenous American cultures.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Center Paracas and Nazca authorship in any description; engage with Peruvian institutions (e.g. the Ministry of Culture) on heritage matters.
